pageData.title: The Viceroyalty of New Granada
pageData.para1: The Viceroyalty of New Granada. The Viceroyalty of New Granada was one of the principal colonial administrative changes effected by the Bourbon monarchs of Spain - a viceroyalty first established in 1717, suppressed in 1723, and reestablished in 1739, taking in present-day Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Venezuela, with its capital at Santa Fe de Bogota. Its creation reflected the growing population and increasing commerce of northern South America, as the Bourbon crown reshaped an empire that had long been ruled from Lima. This viceroyalty matters because it drew the political map from which the modern nations of the north of the continent would emerge.
pageData.para2: New Granada sat within a hierarchical system of colonial government, with the Crown and the Council of the Indies at the top and, moving downward, the viceroy, the audiencias, mayors, and local councils - a system designed to extract wealth while keeping officials in check. The Council of the Indies made colonial and ecclesiastical appointments, fixed the geographical scope of expeditions, and heard appeal cases from the colonial audiencias. The viceroy had overall responsibility for his jurisdiction and resided in the viceregal capital, but could not pass local legislation - though he could serve as president of the audiencia in his capital - that being the responsibility of the individual audiencias, courts with jurisdiction over a particular city and its surrounding area. The audiencia is thus the prime example of Spain's general approach to colonial government - great faith put in legal codes, and officers rotated to ensure they could not be easily corrupted. It was in this ordered world of viceroys and judges that the independence generation of Bolivar and Santander would grow up.

pageData.title: The Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata
pageData.para1: The Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata. The Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata was Spain's fourth and last American viceroyalty - after New Spain, Peru, and New Granada - established in 1776 with its capital at Buenos Aires and including the territory now comprising Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Bolivia. The decision to carve it out of the Viceroyalty of Peru resulted from King Charles III's desire to decentralize the administration of his vast South American empire - and from Spain's wish to curtail the contraband trade flowing between Portuguese Brazil and Buenos Aires. This viceroyalty matters because its creation reshaped the economy of the southern continent and redirected the wealth of the Andes: the silver of the Potosi mines, previously exported via Peru, was now sent through Buenos Aires, and an enormous demand grew for salted meat, especially in Cuba. Its first viceroy, Pedro de Ceballos, pushed the Portuguese back and organized the new government in Buenos Aires before being supplanted by another viceroy just a few months later.
pageData.para2: The new capital thrived, and its people grew in confidence. When the British invaded Buenos Aires in 1806 and again in 1807, the viceroy twice fled - and twice the Creole population of the city successfully fought off the invaders on its own. That experience gave the Creoles confidence in their ability to govern and defend themselves, and in 1810, in the May Revolution, they created a provisional junta and exiled the viceroy. The youngest of Spain's viceroyalties thus became the cradle of Argentine independence, and the territories it had gathered - the pampas, the Paraguayan heartland, and the silver highlands of Upper Peru - went their separate ways into nationhood.

pageData.title: Colonial Brazil
pageData.para1: Colonial Brazil. Colonial Brazil began with a wide turn at sea: in 1500, Pedro Alvares Cabral, commanding an imposing armada bound for India on sailing directions drawn up by da Gama himself, bore so far to the west that on April 22 he sighted the mainland of South America. The Treaty of Tordesillas had divided the New World between Spanish and Portuguese claims, and the region Cabral sighted lay well within the Portuguese zone; the crown promptly claimed it. Whether the landfall was pure accident or quietly planned by the ever-secretive Portuguese, Cabral stayed eight days at Baia Cabralia, where he met Amerindians, before sailing on. Brazil matters because Portugal's accidental landfall grew into the largest colony of South America - a land that would be, at one time or another, the world's leading producer of sugar, diamonds, and tobacco.
pageData.para2: Colonized from the 1530s, Brazil was organized in 1533 into fifteen hereditary captaincies, or fiefs, each extending about fifty leagues along the coast; the captain-generals wielded extensive rights and privileges, but only two of the captaincies were ultimately successful - Sao Vicente, in present Sao Paulo state, and Pernambuco in the northeast. Pernambuco, centered on the town of Olinda, became under its donatario Duarte Coelho Pereira a great sugar-producing region, offering the first example of a profitable agrarian economy in the colony; by the mid-16th century the two successful captaincies had a combined population of only about 5,000. From those modest beginnings - sugar estates worked increasingly by enslaved Africans, coastal towns, and frontier expeditions - would grow the continent's Portuguese-speaking giant. The Crown appointed a governor in 1549 to bring order to the colony, which became an official viceroyalty later divided in two, with Salvador the capital of the north and Rio de Janeiro of the south. Sugar's labor demands drove the slave trade: after the enslaving of Amerindians was prohibited from 1570, most enslaved workers came by ship from Africa, particularly Portuguese Angola - 150,000 during sugar's peak from 1600 to 1625 alone - and the result was a great mixing of Europeans, Amerindians, and Africans, more so than in any other Portuguese colony.

pageData.title: Gran Colombia
pageData.para1: Gran Colombia. Gran Colombia was the republic formed in the heat of the independence wars from the territories of the Viceroyalty of New Granada - roughly the modern nations of Colombia, Panama, Venezuela, and Ecuador. In 1819, in the context of their war for independence, the patriots set up a regular government at a congress in Angostura - now Ciudad Bolivar, Venezuela - and the republic was definitely organized at the Congress of Cucuta on August 30, 1821 - a conglomerate of recently freed countries formerly part of the viceroyalty, liberated section by section, with its capital at Bogota: Simon Bolivar became president and Francisco de Paula Santander vice president, under a constitution calling for a bicameral legislature. Gran Colombia matters because it was the boldest experiment of the independence era - the dream of holding the liberated north together as one great nation.
pageData.para2: The experiment did not hold. Rivalry for public office and regional jealousies led to a rebellion in Venezuela in 1826; after ruling as dictator from 1828 to 1830, Bolivar convoked a convention that produced a new constitution, but it was recognized only in Nueva Granada - Colombia and Panama - as Venezuela and Ecuador went their own way. Bolivar resigned and left for the northern coast, where he died, his uniform decorated with the medals of his campaigns: the Order of the Liberators of Venezuela, the Cross of Boyaca, and the Liberators of Cundinamarca. Gran Colombia dissolved in 1830, its member territories becoming the separate nations that stand today. Its short life left a lasting question for the continent: unity or fragmentation - a question the new republics answered differently, one by one.

pageData.title: The Viceroyalty of Peru
pageData.para1: The Viceroyalty of Peru. The Viceroyalty of Peru was established in 1542 as Spain's second viceroyalty in the Americas, and at its height it encompassed part or all of modern-day Venezuela, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Paraguay, Uruguay, and Argentina - nearly the whole of Spanish South America. Its capital was assigned to Lima, the coastal city founded by Pizarro in 1535. The viceroyalty was born from conquest: it was in Cajamarca that Atahualpa had agreed to fill a room - seventeen feet wide and eight feet high - with gold and silver as ransom for his freedom, a moment captured in the famous colonial image of the Inka asked what the Spaniard eats, and answering: gold, and Spanish colonial rule in the Andes was only consolidated with the execution of Tupac Amaru, the last ruler of the Neo-Inka state, a semi-autonomous faction that held out after the empire's fall. This viceroyalty matters because for two and a half centuries it was the administrative heart of Spain's South American empire.
pageData.para2: Peru was more than a machinery of extraction: a vibrant artistic culture emerged throughout the viceroyalty's major cities, each a hotbed of artistic activity - Lima, the old Inca capital of Cuzco, and Arequipa in present-day Peru, and Quito in present-day Ecuador - where indigenous, European, and African traditions met in painting, sculpture, and architecture. From its Andean silver to its viceregal court, Peru set the pattern of Spanish rule on the continent, until the Bourbon reforms of the 18th century carved New Granada and the Rio de la Plata from its flanks and the wars of independence brought the viceregal age to an end.

pageData.title: The Spanish American Wars of Independence
pageData.para1: The Spanish-American Wars of Independence. The Spanish-American Wars of Independence had their harbinger in the Andes: on November 4, 1780, Tupac Amaru II - a kuraka of royal Inca blood - rose against the corregidor Arriaga, claiming to act under orders from the Spanish crown, and days later decreed the abolition of slavery for Black people, the first such decree in Spanish America, before his rebellion was crushed. The wars proper began with a collapse at the center: when Napoleon seized Spain and the Central Junta dissolved in January 1810, new juntas appeared across Spanish America, from Caracas on April 19 onward. In Mexico the revolt took the form of rebellion under Miguel Hidalgo, captured and executed in 1811, though resistance outlived him. These wars matter because they broke three centuries of Spanish rule and made a dozen nations.
pageData.para2: The wars were won by two great converging campaigns. From the south, Jose de San Martin raised the Army of the Andes in Cuyo, led the audacious Crossing of the Andes into Chile, and triumphed at Chacabuco and Maipu, becoming the Liberator of Argentina, Chile, and Peru. From the north, Simon Bolivar freed Venezuela and New Granada, forming Gran Colombia. When the two liberators met behind closed doors at the Guayaquil conference on July 26-27, 1822, San Martin withdrew from the scene and Bolivar took over the task of fully liberating Peru. The end came high in the Andes: on December 9, 1824, at the Battle of Ayacucho, Bolivar's lieutenant Antonio Jose de Sucre defeated the royalist army, and Viceroy Jose de la Serna, wounded, surrendered - while Sucre's campaign continued through 1825 in Upper Peru. Spain's continental empire was finished.

pageData.title: The Empire of Brazil
pageData.para1: The Empire of Brazil. The Empire of Brazil was born from a royal family in exile: when the Portuguese court crossed the Atlantic, Brazilians welcomed Dom Joao, who promptly abolished the Portuguese commercial monopoly on Brazilian trade and opened the colony's ports. But antagonism grew between Portuguese and Brazilians, republican propagandists gained influence, and when the Cortes demanded the young prince Pedro return to Portugal, most Brazilians supported his decision to stay. In January 1822 he formed a ministry headed by Jose Bonifacio de Andrada e Silva - a distinguished Paulista scholar later known as the Patriarch of Independence - and on September 7, on the plain of Ipiranga near Sao Paulo, he proclaimed the independence of Brazil. Portugal acknowledged it in 1825. The Empire matters because it gave South America's largest nation a strikingly orderly independence: a monarchy, not a republic, for nearly seven decades.
pageData.para2: Pedro I's popularity declined after he lost the Cisplatine province - now Uruguay - in a costly war, and under pressure he formally abdicated in 1831, leaving a child emperor and years of regency: from 1831 to 1835 a triple regency tried in vain to end civil warfare in the provinces. Under Pedro II, crowned young, Brazil found stability: relations with the United States and Europe were generally cordial, and the emperor himself visited Europe in 1871, 1876, and 1888. The era was marked by the bloody Paraguayan War - the War of the Triple Alliance of 1864-70, in which Brazil, allied with Argentina and Uruguay, prevailed - and by the slow death of slavery: the slave trade, promised away in 1831, did not completely cease for another twenty years, antislavery agitation began in the 1860s, and in 1871 Brazil enacted the Law of the Free Womb on the long road to abolition.
